articles.title: A home for people building with term-llm
articles.excerpt: Terminal-first. Browser-ready. Built together. A place for the workflows, questions, and small discoveries that make an open-source tool better.
articles.raw:
term-llm starts with a straightforward idea: **your workflow should not belong to one model provider.** Choose the model, give it the right tools, and keep the work close to your projects.

This blog and community are a home for the people putting that idea into practice. Not a wall of launch announcements. A place to explain what works, be precise about what does not, and build better habits together.

## One project, more than one way to work

Use the terminal for a quick question, a shell pipeline, or a focused conversation. Open the browser workspace when the work calls for persistent sessions, projects, worktrees, diffs, and a shell alongside your agent.

```sh
term-llm serve web
```

The interface changes. The principle does not: make the work visible, reviewable, and yours.

## What belongs here

- **Questions with context.** Include the command, provider, version, and what you expected. Remove API keys and private material before posting.
- **Workflows people can try.** A small agent instruction, a useful pipe, or an MCP integration is worth sharing. Explain permissions and trade-offs, not just the happy path.
- **Constructive disagreement.** A local model, a hosted API, and a supported subscription can each be the right choice for different work. Tell us about the task, not just the leaderboard.
- **Contributions of every size.** Reproduction steps and clearer documentation matter as much as code.

## Start with the next useful thing

If you are new, [follow the quickstart](https://term-llm.com/getting-started/quickstart/). If you have something working, share the smallest version another person could reproduce. For source, issues, and pull requests, [visit GitHub](https://github.com/SamSaffron/term-llm).

The article is the beginning. **What is one task you would like term-llm to make easier?**
replies: A useful workflow post should include the command, the model connection, and the permissions it needs. That would make examples much easier to reproduce.
Could we keep a collection of small, read-only examples for people trying agents for the first time? Reviewing a diff seems like a good starting point.
That is a useful direction for the Workflows category: one task, one reproducible example, and an honest note about the limitations.

articles.title: From terminal to workspace, without changing tools
articles.excerpt: A command for a quick question. A workspace for a longer task. How projects, worktrees, and visible diffs change the way you work with an agent.
articles.raw:
Some tasks belong in a pipe. Others need a place to spread out. term-llm supports both: a terminal interface for focused work and a browser workspace served from your own machine.

## Start with a small command

A staged diff already contains useful context. You can pass it to an agent without copying it into a chat window:

```sh
git diff --staged | term-llm ask @commit-message
```

For a read-only review, the built-in reviewer is another starting point:

```sh
term-llm ask @reviewer "review the staged changes"
```

Read the response critically. An agent review is another pair of eyes, not a guarantee that the code is correct.

## Open a workspace when the task grows

```sh
term-llm serve web
```

The browser interface brings persistent conversations, project organization, worktrees, live file diffs, and an interactive shell into one working environment. The release binary includes the interface; there is no separate frontend build to assemble.

The important shift is from a transcript to a project. You can see what changed, inspect the diff, run checks, and decide what to keep. Isolated Git worktrees help separate parallel experiments without treating every agent change as ready to merge.

## Keep the handoff explicit

A good working loop is small:

1. Describe the task and the boundaries.
2. Let the agent inspect the relevant context.
3. Review the proposed changes and run the appropriate checks.
4. Decide what to commit or discard.

An agent can help do the work, but choosing an interface should not take that decision away from you.

## Before exposing a workspace

A browser interface is not automatically a public service. Follow the [web workspace deployment and authentication guidance](https://term-llm.com/guides/web-ui-and-api/) before making it reachable beyond your machine. The workspace is a shared operator security domain, not a multi-tenant hosting platform.

**Where do you prefer to switch from the terminal to a browser, and why?**
replies: The staged-diff example is a good small first step. I would still check the generated commit message against the actual diff, especially if there are several unrelated changes.
Worktrees are the part I want to understand better. How do people decide whether a second agent needs an isolated worktree or can safely inspect the same checkout?

Read-only inspection and concurrent editing have different risks. For an editing experiment, a separate worktree makes the changes easier to review and discard. It does not replace tests or a careful merge.
A walkthrough that ends with reviewing and discarding an experiment would be useful. Tutorials often show the successful path but not how to back out cleanly.

articles.title: Local runtime, local model: know the difference
articles.excerpt: Running an AI tool on your machine is not the same as keeping every request local. Follow the model, tools, and review path before choosing your setup.
articles.raw:
“Runs on your machine” answers one question: where does the application execute? It does not answer where your prompts, files, search queries, or tool results go.

term-llm is a local, self-hostable runtime. It can connect to hosted APIs, supported subscriptions, or local model servers. Those choices have different data paths.

## Follow the model request

With a hosted provider, the context you send goes to that provider. With a local model through Ollama or LM Studio, inference can stay on your machine. That is an important distinction, but it is only the first layer.

Check the [provider setup guide](https://term-llm.com/getting-started/providers-and-setup/) for the connection you intend to use. Availability, capabilities, and third-party terms can change.

## Follow the tools, too

A local model can still use a tool that reaches an external service. Search, an MCP server, media generation, or a separately configured Guardian review path may involve another destination.

Before processing sensitive material, ask:

- Which model receives the conversation context?
- Which files can the agent read?
- Which tools can contact other services?
- Where does approval or Guardian review happen?
- What is stored in sessions and logs?

A local inference endpoint is not, by itself, an offline-mode guarantee.

## Permissions should match the task

Start with the smallest useful permissions. A reviewer generally needs to inspect a diff, not rewrite the repository. A developer may need file edits and a test command, but those are distinct capabilities. Workspace grants for file tools do not authorize shell commands.

Read the [built-in tool and approval documentation](https://term-llm.com/reference/built-in-tools/#approval-modes) before broadening access. Human approval and Guardian-reviewed auto mode are choices to understand, not labels to assume are equivalent.

## Choose deliberately

Hosted and local models are tools with different strengths, costs, and operational constraints. The useful question is not which one wins in the abstract. It is which configuration fits this task and this data.

**What do you check before giving an agent access to a new project?**
replies: The distinction between the runtime and the inference endpoint is worth making explicit. A privacy checklist should include MCP and search, not only the provider setting.
Could workflow recipes list their external connections alongside the required permissions? That would help someone decide whether an example is suitable for a private repository.
Yes—model, tools, and review routing all belong in that explanation. Avoid posting credentials or private project content when asking for help with a configuration.
A read-only starting point would help here too. First verify which context is being sent, then add editing or shell access only when the task needs it.

topics: Help
Start here: your first term-llm session

Follow the [quickstart](https://term-llm.com/getting-started/quickstart/) and tell us where you get stuck. Include your operating system, term-llm version, provider, and the command you ran. Remove secrets from logs.
Workflows
Introduce yourself and the task you want to automate
What kind of work brought you to term-llm? Tell us about one small task you would like to make easier—no polished demo required.
Workflows
Share a useful shell pipeline
Have an example that sends existing context to an agent? Share the command, what it consumes, and how you check the output. Note any external services involved.
Workflows
What belongs in a read-only reviewer agent?
A focused review is easier to evaluate than a request to find everything. What instructions and boundaries help you get useful feedback on a diff?
Help
Provider setup: what to include in a support question

Include the provider name, authentication method (not the credential), version, exact error, and a minimal reproduction. See [providers and setup](https://term-llm.com/getting-started/providers-and-setup/).
Help
Ollama and LM Studio: share a reproducible setup
Document the model, server configuration, hardware constraints, and a small task someone else can try. Local inference does not necessarily make connected tools local.
Workflows
When do you open the browser workspace?
What work benefits from persistent sessions, diffs, and a shell in one view? What do you prefer to keep in a terminal pipeline?
Workflows
Projects and worktrees: keeping experiments separate
How would you organize concurrent agent tasks so their changes remain easy to inspect? Share a small example and explain the review and merge step.
Help
Understanding approvals before enabling more tools
Which part of the [approval model](https://term-llm.com/reference/built-in-tools/#approval-modes) would you like explained? File grants and shell authorization are separate boundaries.
Workflows
MCP integrations worth documenting
Describe the tool, the task it helps with, and the data it sends or stores. A minimal setup and a note about permissions make an integration easier to evaluate.
Workflows
Small jobs you would like to schedule
What recurring work would benefit from an agent job? Describe the inputs, success checks, and how failures should be reported. Start with a non-destructive task.
Help
Choosing a model for the task, not the leaderboard
What capabilities matter for your workflow: tool use, context, latency, vision, or cost? Share a reproducible task rather than a general ranking.
Help
Before making the web workspace remotely accessible
Read the [deployment guidance](https://term-llm.com/guides/web-ui-and-api/). Discuss authentication, HTTPS, and network boundaries without sharing credentials. This is not a multi-tenant platform.
Workflows
Widget ideas for a useful workspace
What small view or interaction would make a project easier to work on? See the [widget guide](https://term-llm.com/guides/widgets/) and describe a focused use case.
Help
Usage tracking: what would you like to understand?
Which questions do you want usage records to answer? Token counts, estimated prices, and provider coverage are not the same thing. Include the model and task when comparing results.
Workflows
What do you check before committing an agent's changes?
Share a review checklist. Tests, a careful diff, and checking unintended file changes are useful starting points. What task-specific checks do you add?
Development
Writing a bug report someone can reproduce

Include version, operating system, provider, minimal steps, expected behavior, and actual behavior. Redact secrets. Confirmed bugs and pull requests belong in [GitHub](https://github.com/SamSaffron/term-llm).
Development
Documentation improvements: where did you hesitate?
Which instruction required guesswork? Link to the page, describe the ambiguity, and suggest an example that would have helped. Small corrections count.
Feedback
Feature ideas: begin with the problem
Describe the workflow you are trying to complete and what is difficult today. A small example and the alternatives you considered are more useful than a large feature list.
Development
A contributor's first small change
Interested in contributing? Start by reading the repository's current contribution guidance. Reproductions, tests, and documentation are good ways to learn the code without taking on a large feature.
